ASD characteristics and social behaviors are different in individuals with Angelman syndrome, Cornelia deLange syndrome, and Cri duChat (5 p) syndrome.

the proportion of individuals meeting cutoff for autism spectrum disorder (as measured by the Social Communication Questionnaires) was significantly higher in Angelman and Cornelia de Lange syndromes than in Cri du Chat syndrome.
the social behavior of individuals with Angelman syndrome, Cornelia de lange syndrome and Cri du Chat syndrome (also known as 5p syndrome) is distinct.

social behavior and autism spectrum disorder ( ASD) in genetic syndromic conditions.
the social behavior of individuals with genetic disorders.
the social behavior of children and adults with autism spectrum disorder ( ASD ) and the social behavior of their parents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the social behavior profiles of individuals with CdLS, CdCS and AS differ from each other and from the social behavior profiles reported in individuals with typical development.
the ASD symptoms in CdCS are less prominent than those in CdLS and AS.
the social behavior of individuals with AS, CdLS, and CdCS are distinct and that these differences may be related to their respective underlying etiologies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ASD characteristics and social behavior vary across genetic syndromes and may be influenced by the genetic etiology.
the ASD phenotype is heterogeneous and is influenced by the specific genetic syndrome.
the ASD characteristics of social motivation and communication are significantly different in CdLS and CdCS compared with AS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ASD and social behavior are not necessarily related in genetic syndromic conditions.
social behaviors and characteristics of autism are different for individuals with Angelman, Cornia de Lange, and 5p syndrome.
ASD and social behavior profiles are distinct across these three genetic syndromes, and that these profiles are not simply the sum of the social impairments associated with the syndromes themselves.
